drivers.title: Demand recovery met tighter export supply
drivers.text: Lynas linked the price surge to recovering demand after the financial crisis and tighter Chinese export supply. Its 2010 report also explained how export tariffs and VAT widened export-versus-domestic prices.
drivers.scope: Producer interpretation of this historical episode; not an independently estimated policy effect.

drivers.title: Inventories and manufacturing demand changed
drivers.text: Lynas attributed the retracement to manufacturing-efficiency changes, customer inventory de-stocking and softer macroeconomic conditions.
drivers.scope: A contemporaneous producer account; it does not quantify each driver’s contribution.

drivers.title: Supply enforcement and spot buying interacted
drivers.text: Arafura’s study attributed the NdPr rebound to quota pressure, reduced illegal mining/processing, environmental inspections and speculative spot purchases.
drivers.scope: Reported explanation in a 2019 project study, not a causal model or a present-day forecast.

drivers.title: Iron ore responds to a different demand system
drivers.text: The World Bank linked iron-ore weakness to Chinese property and construction demand, port inventories and ample Australian/Brazilian supply; new West African capacity was prospective pressure.
drivers.scope: Dated analysis and outlook; it does not establish the cause of September’s observed price.

drivers.title: Operating output is not market demand
drivers.text: Rio Tinto attributed stronger borate output to robust market conditions and disclosed a strategic review of Borates. Its quarterly tonnes remain one producer’s B₂O₃ output.
drivers.scope: Producer commentary, not measured global boron demand or magnet-grade FeB output.
